stem: A support agent has run for 60 turns. The MLflow trace shows the message history growing every turn, with old tool outputs and greetings still in the prompt. The agent now ignores the customer's latest constraint and repeats steps it finished earlier. Which technique addresses this failure most directly?

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the agent varies its steps instead of repeating the ones it has already done
Move to a model with a larger context window and keep the full history unchanged, so nothing has to be removed from the prompt
Delete every message older than the last five turns, since earlier turns rarely matter once the conversation has moved on
Compact the older turns into a short state note holding decisions, open items and constraints, and keep the latest turns verbatim

stem: A sales assistant calls a Unity Catalog SQL function, `get_orders`, that returns every column of every order for a customer. The trace shows that call as the largest span, and later answers cite the wrong order because the useful rows are lost in the output. Which change addresses the cause?

choices.text: Change the function to take a date range and a row limit and return only the columns the answer needs
Replace the SQL function with a Python function that returns the same full rows, because Python results are summarized automatically
Ask the model in the system prompt to "ignore irrelevant order columns" while leaving the function output unchanged
Cache the full function output in the session so the model does not have to call the function a second time

stem: A personal-assistant agent re-asks every user for their preferred report format and time zone in each new conversation. Raw transcripts of past chats are kept in a session store. Which two changes best fit the failure? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep the preferences only in the in-context conversation history of the current conversation and its prompt
Keep the memories scoped to the user they describe, so recall returns that user's preferences and no one else's
Delete the session store, because a session is the only place where memory can be kept between chats
Paste every past transcript of the user into the system prompt at the start of each new conversation
Store the stable preferences as durable facts in an agent memory store, and let the agent recall them by semantic search when relevant

stem: A research agent browses many web pages in the same context as its planning notes. After a few searches, the trace shows tens of thousands of tokens of raw page text, and the plan itself is no longer being followed. The team wants to keep the planner's context clean. Which technique fits best?

choices.text: Let the planner keep all raw pages and add an instruction to focus on the plan and skip unrelated text
Reduce the number of searches to one per run, so the planner never has to read more than a single page
Hand each search to a sub-agent with its own context, which returns only a short, sourced summary
Store each raw page in the planner's notes under a title, so that the planner can scroll back to any page

stem: A customer-service agent has this in its prompt: a rule "keep every answer under two sentences" and, further down, a rule "always list the full policy clause, the date and the exception rules". Traces show answers that are sometimes short and sometimes long for the same request. Which fix targets the cause?

choices.text: Add a third rule saying "when in doubt, follow the most recent instruction" and leave both existing rules in place
Add several few-shot examples of long answers, so the model sees that the longer rule is the one that usually applies
Rewrite the two rules into one instruction that states which wins and when, with a single answer format
Raise the maximum output tokens so the longer rule can always be satisfied without being cut off

stem: A code-migration agent writes a 12-item plan at the start of a run. After about 40 tool calls the trace shows the plan far back in the prompt, below pages of tool output, and the agent starts skipping items and declaring the job done early. Which technique targets this failure?

choices.text: Keep a short task list that the agent updates each step, and place the current list at the end of the context
Delete all tool outputs after each call so the plan is the only thing left, and the agent has no results to build on
Raise the maximum number of steps in the run, so the agent has more chances to come back to the skipped items
Repeat the original plan at the very top of the prompt a second time, so the model sees it twice before the tool outputs

stem: A log-analysis agent must answer questions about incident reports stored in Unity Catalog volumes. Loading every report into the prompt would fill the window before the first question. Which proactive strategy reduces context pressure while keeping every report reachable?

choices.text: Summarize every report once into a single paragraph and keep only those paragraphs, discarding the original files
Keep an index of report IDs and titles in context, plus a tool that loads one report when details are needed
Split each report into sentences and load all sentences in random order, so no single report takes up much space
Load the five newest reports at the start of every run, as recent incidents are likeliest to be asked

stem: An analytics agent has 28 tools, and every model call includes all their definitions. Its SQL tool also returns whole result sets. The team wants proactive measures before quality drops. Which two apply? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Expose all 28 tools at every step, because the model needs to see the full list to decide when none apply
Merge all 28 tools into one tool with a long free-text parameter that accepts any request
Pass SQL result sets unchanged so that the model sees every row, then ask it to pick the relevant ones
Give each task only the few tools it needs, instead of the full set of 28
Scope tool results: aggregate in SQL or limit rows and columns so the tool returns only what the question needs

stem: A team registers an external MCP server in the workspace so its agent can use it. The server exposes many tools, but this agent's job needs only three of them. Governance lets the team share access and restrict which tools are available. Which choice best reduces context pressure?

choices.text: Restrict the registered server to the three tools the agent needs, so only those definitions reach the model
Disable tool calling and let the agent describe what it would have called, to be run by hand afterwards
Register the server separately once for every tool, so the agent loads each tool definition one at a time
Leave all tools available, and add a system-prompt line telling the agent which three to use and to skip the rest

stem: An agent with Databricks agent memory has accumulated hundreds of stored facts about one user. The current design injects all of them into the system prompt at the start of every conversation, and latency and costs have risen. Which strategy fits best?

choices.text: Keep injecting all memories but sort them alphabetically so the model can find the one it needs more quickly
Retrieve by semantic search only the few memories relevant to the current request and add those to the context
Move all the memories into the conversation history, so they are summarized together with the chat turns
Truncate the stored memories to the first sentence of each, and inject all of them at the start as before

stem: A documentation agent has an AI Search retriever tool. Its trace shows the agent calling the retriever on every turn, including greetings and arithmetic questions, and adding five chunks each time. What is the best proactive change to the tool's configuration?

choices.text: Increase the number of chunks returned, so each call is more likely to contain something the agent can use
Remove the tool description entirely, so the model stops associating the tool with documentation questions
Write a tool description that says when to search (product documentation questions) and when not to
Set the retriever to run before every model call, so the cost of searching is paid in a single predictable place

stem: A finance agent trace shows: step 3, a tool returns "Q3 revenue: 4.2M" from a stale cache of last year's data; steps 5, 7 and 9, the agent's reasoning cites "revenue is 4.2M" as an established fact, and the final report is wrong even though a later tool call returned the correct 6.1M. Which context failure does this show?

choices.text: Context clash, because two sources were retrieved from different vendors and the agent chose the cheaper one
Context distraction, because the context grew long enough that the agent over-weights its accumulated history over the task
Context confusion, because too many unrelated tools were defined and the agent chose the wrong source
Context poisoning, because an incorrect value entered the context and was then reused as if it were true

stem: A data-migration agent has been running for several hours. Its trace shows a very large message history in which every statement is accurate and consistent. In recent steps the agent keeps repeating actions it completed in the first hour and has stopped working on the current subtask. Which context failure explains this best?

choices.text: Context clash, because first-hour instructions contradict the instructions of the current subtask
Context poisoning, because an inaccurate statement from the first hour was reused in the plan
Context confusion, because the agent has too many near-identical tools and keeps choosing the wrong one
Context distraction, because the long history pulls the agent toward repeating past actions

stem: A helpdesk agent was given 45 tools, including `create_ticket`, `create_ticket_draft`, `update_ticket` and `log_ticket_note`, with near-identical descriptions. In the trace, when asked only to draft a ticket for review, the agent calls `create_ticket`, which files it right away. All the tool results were correct. Which context failure does this show?

choices.text: Context confusion, because overlapping, superfluous tool definitions steered the model to the wrong tool
Context clash, because the user's request contradicts the system prompt about whether tickets may be filed
Context poisoning, because an earlier tool result put a false fact into the history
Context distraction, because the conversation is long enough that the agent forgets what it was asked to do

stem: A policy-answering agent retrieves two documents for one question: a 2023 handbook that says refunds are allowed within 30 days, and a 2025 handbook that says 14 days. In the trace, the final answer says 30 days in one sentence and 14 days in the next. Which context failure does this show?

choices.text: Context poisoning, because the 2025 handbook is a hallucination that the agent repeated several times
Context clash, because two retrieved sources contradict each other and the model has no rule for which wins
Context confusion, because the retriever returned too many tools for the agent to choose between
Context distraction, because the retrieved text is so long that the agent loses track of the question asked

stem: A planning assistant has agent memory. One day it hallucinated "the user's budget is 50k" during a chat, and a memory pipeline distilled that into a stored memory. Over the next weeks, in separate conversations, the agent keeps proposing 50k plans and cites the stored memory. Which diagnosis and remedy fit best?

choices.text: Context distraction; shorten the system prompt so that the stored memories take a smaller share of the window
Context clash; add an instruction telling the agent to prefer its own opinion over stored memories
Context poisoning that persists in memory; correct or delete the bad memory and validate what the pipeline writes
Context confusion; remove tools from the agent until it only answers budget questions

stem: A team is building a customer agent with these needs: the conversation must resume after the agent restarts, and the agent should remember each customer's preferences in later conversations. Which Databricks capability supplies this state?

choices.text: A Genie Agent that stores the conversation as sample questions for future users
Agent sessions and agent memory, both managed stores backed by Lakebase
MLflow Tracing, by replaying each stored trace as the agent's memory of the customer
Unity Catalog tags on the customer table, which the agent reads at the start of each conversation

stem: A team registers an MCP server in the workspace for several agents. Security needs to decide which groups may use it, to manage the credentials it needs, and to monitor how it is used. Which Databricks capability covers this?

choices.text: MLflow Tracing, by granting each group access to the spans that the server's tool calls produce
Lakebase, by storing the credentials and a usage log for the server in a Postgres table the agents read
AI Search, by indexing the server's tool descriptions so that only authorized groups can retrieve them
Unity Gateway, which controls access, manages credentials and monitors usage for registered MCP servers

stem: A platform team wrote a Python function that checks an order's refund eligibility. Several agents should call it as a tool, and only members of the support group may run it. Where should the function live?

choices.text: In Unity Catalog as a function, with EXECUTE granted to the support group
Inside each agent's prompt as a code block, so the model can rewrite it per request
In a Lakebase table named after the function, with a row per call to hold the result
In an MLflow experiment as a logged artifact that each agent downloads at start-up

stem: A deployed agent costs more per request and responds slower than during testing. The team wants to see, for each step of a request (model call, retriever, tool), the inputs, outputs, latency and token usage to find the step to fix. Which Databricks capability gives this view?

choices.text: Unity Catalog lineage, which shows which tables and functions the agent touched during a request
AI Search, by indexing the agent's logs and querying them by semantic similarity
MLflow Tracing, which records inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every intermediate step
Lakebase, by logging each request to a Postgres table through a custom tool call

stem: An architect compares MCP options for an agent in a Databricks workspace. Which two statements are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The Databricks SQL MCP server is recommended for open-ended natural-language business questions, because it hides SQL from the agent
Databricks-provided MCPs ignore Unity Catalog permissions, so access is controlled only in the agent's own code
The Genie Agent MCP is the right choice for any question across the whole workspace, and its calls are governed by Unity Gateway policies

The Genie One MCP server is the recommended choice for natural-language analytics across the workspace, and it is governed through Unity Gateway grants and policies plus the underlying resource permissions
A Genie Agent MCP is scoped to one curated Genie Agent, using its tables, instructions and examples, and its calls bypass Unity Gateway governance

stem: A classification agent's prompt carries 30 few-shot examples, most near-copies of each other covering the same two easy categories. The trace shows the examples are 70 percent of the prompt tokens, and the rare categories are still misclassified. Which change improves focus?

choices.text: Keep the 30 examples but repeat the category list after each one, so the categories stay in front of the model
Replace them with a handful of diverse, canonical examples that include the rare categories, and drop the near-copies
Move all 30 examples into the system prompt, so the model treats them as rules instead of examples
Add 30 more examples of the rare categories after the existing ones, so that every category is covered by many examples

stem: An MLflow trace of one request shows these token counts per span: system prompt 1,200; retriever result 9,800 (ten chunks, the answer used two); model call 1,000; final answer 250. The team wants to improve focus without hurting recall. Which change fits?

choices.text: Remove the retriever and let the model answer from its own knowledge, which removes the largest span
Shorten the system prompt to 300 tokens, since it is the only part of the context that the team writes by hand
Return fewer, better-ranked chunks by lowering the result count, and return only the columns the answer needs
Cap the final answer at 100 tokens so that the whole request uses less of the budget

stem: A system prompt for a travel-booking agent has 40 numbered rules. Thirty-four cover rare edge cases (lost passport, group bookings, strikes) that apply to a few percent of requests, and answers to common requests have become less consistent. Which change improves focus?

choices.text: Keep the core rules in the prompt and load the edge-case guidance on demand, only when the request matches the situation
Rewrite each of the 34 edge-case rules in capital letters so that they stand out when the situation arises
Add a rule at the top saying that the first six rules matter most and that the remaining rules apply only if they are relevant
Move all 40 rules to the end of the prompt, since models pay the most attention to the end of the context

stem: Traces for a research agent show two contributors to its high token use: each turn re-sends the full verbatim history including every earlier tool output, and the SQL tool returns complete result sets. Which two changes improve focus? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Re-send the full history every turn but sort the older tool outputs by size so the largest are read first
Raise the maximum output tokens so the agent can write longer answers that use up more of the history
Replace older tool outputs in the history with short summaries or references, and keep recent turns verbatim
Add a second SQL tool that returns the same whole result sets so the model can compare them
Make the SQL tool return aggregates or a limited, column-trimmed result rather than whole result sets

stem: An agent has two retriever tools, one over product manuals and one over support articles. For many questions both return the same chunk of text, and the trace shows the duplicate chunk appearing twice in the prompt, along with its repeated neighbors. What change improves focus?

choices.text: Increase the number of results from each retriever so the duplicates are diluted by additional passages
De-duplicate retrieved chunks before they are added to the context, so each distinct passage appears once
Ask the model in the prompt to treat repeated passages as especially reliable because they are repeated
Merge the two source indexes into a single index but keep calling both retrievers with the same query

stem: A ticket-triage agent labels each incoming message with one of six categories and extracts the order id. It handles a very high volume. Its traces show extended thinking enabled, and most output tokens of each request go to reasoning. An MLflow evaluation shows the same label accuracy with thinking turned off. Which reasoning mode should this step use?

choices.text: Extended thinking plus worked reasoning chains in the prompt, so the model writes shorter thoughts for each category
Extended thinking with a larger thinking budget, because more reasoning tokens raise accuracy on classification as well
Extended thinking with a smaller maximum output, so the visible label is cut to the shortest possible text
Standard or reduced thinking, because a simple and well-specified task gains nothing from extra reasoning tokens

stem: A nightly agent builds crew shift schedules under many interacting constraints (rest periods, certifications, shift swaps). With the standard mode its short answers often violate one or more constraints, as judged by an MLflow scorer. The job runs overnight, so latency does not matter, and the team has token budget to spare. Which choice fits?

choices.text: Use extended thinking for the planning call with a budget sized for the constraint checks
Use reduced thinking and split the schedule into one call per crew member so each answer is short
Keep the standard mode and repeat the full constraint list three times in the user turn so it receives more attention
Keep the standard mode and raise the temperature so the model explores more candidate schedules in its single answer

stem: A team enables extended thinking on `databricks-claude-sonnet-4-5` through the Anthropic Messages API, with `budget_tokens` set to 8000 and `max_tokens` also set to 8000. The request is rejected, and even a request that ran would leave no room for the visible answer after the reasoning. Which change fits?

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` above the thinking budget, leaving room for the visible answer after the reasoning tokens
Remove the thinking setting entirely and expect the same reasoning depth from the standard mode
Lower `max_tokens` further, so the model is forced to think more briefly and still answers within the limit
Write "think for 8,000 tokens" in the system prompt and leave both numeric settings unchanged

stem: A migration assistant runs three steps per request: (1) rewrite the user message into a standalone search query, (2) plan a multi-system migration with dependent actions, (3) answer a short factual follow-up from retrieved text. The team can set the reasoning mode for each step. Which two assignments fit best? (Select TWO)

choices.text: No thinking for the migration-planning step, to keep the window free for the tool outputs of the migration
Extended thinking for the query-rewriting step, because every step of a pipeline should use the deepest mode available
Reduced or no thinking for the query-rewriting step, which is short, well specified and runs on every request
Extended thinking for the short factual answer, so the model re-derives the retrieved facts before it replies
Extended thinking, or a high effort setting, for the migration-planning step, where a wrong ordering of dependent actions is costly

stem: An agent's context is 90% tool output from three verbose SQL calls, and it now answers from the wrong table. A teammate proposes switching on extended thinking so the model will "reason past" the irrelevant rows. Which response is best?

choices.text: Agree, and also have the model restate every tool output inside its thinking so that it can compare all of them
Cut the tool output first (needed columns and rows only, old outputs cleared), then add thinking only if still needed
Disagree, but double `max_tokens` so the model has plenty of space left over after reading all the tool output
Agree: deeper reasoning lets the model ignore irrelevant rows, so the large tool outputs can stay in place as they are

stem: A policy agent places 40 retrieved passages, about 70,000 tokens, in its prompt. An MLflow evaluation shows correct answers when the relevant clause is among the first or last few passages and frequent misses when it sits in the middle, although the model's window is far from full. Which change addresses this most directly?

choices.text: Raise the reasoning effort so the model reads each of the 40 passages in more depth before it answers
Move to a model with a larger window so the 40 passages fit and the middle gets equal attention
Duplicate the full passage list at the end of the prompt, so every clause appears again near the question
Keep a handful of top-ranked passages and put the most relevant one next to the question, instead of all 40

stem: To improve recall, a team raised an agent's retriever from returning 5 chunks to 25. The correct chunk now appears in the returned set in more traces, but the answer correctness score in MLflow evaluation went down, and answers often cite loosely related chunks. Which change should the team make?

choices.text: Return a small number of chunks, add a re-ranker or metadata filter to put the right chunk on top, and re-run the evaluation
Keep 25 chunks and shorten each chunk to one sentence, so the extra chunks cost fewer tokens in the window
Keep 25 chunks and tell the model in the prompt to ignore chunks that are less relevant than the correct one
Return 100 chunks, since recall in the retrieved set was the real objective and correctness will recover with more material

stem: An agent calls its AI Search tool with the entire conversation transcript as the query text. Early in a chat the retrieved chunks are on topic; after dozens of turns they drift toward unrelated subjects that appeared earlier in the chat. Which change restores retrieval quality?

choices.text: Increase the chunk overlap in the index so each chunk repeats more neighbouring text
Increase the number of results returned, so on-topic chunks will appear among the drifting ones
Switch to a larger embedding model, since a long transcript query needs a bigger vector to represent its meaning
Have the agent write a short, self-contained query for the current need and send only that to the retriever

stem: A contract-review agent receives 20 full documents in one prompt and is asked to compare their termination clauses. The answers are shallow and miss clauses from documents in the middle of the set. Which redesign best restores quality while keeping token use moderate?

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the model samples different readings of the 20 documents and picks the longest answer
Extract the termination clauses from each document in separate small calls, then compare the extracts in a final call
Keep all 20 documents and add "read every document carefully" at the start and end
Drop every other document at random, so the set is half as long and the middle gets more attention

stem: A team wants to learn at which context size its agent's accuracy starts to fall, to set a working context budget. They have an MLflow 3 evaluation dataset and scorers, and traces record token counts. Which approach gives a usable answer?

choices.text: Compare only average latency across several prompt sizes, since quality always stays flat until the whole window is full
Use the model's maximum context window as the budget, since the vendor sized it for full use
Run one evaluation at several prompt sizes, padding the same content with realistic extra context, and set the budget where scores drop
Run one evaluation with the longest possible prompt, and if it passes, use that length as the budget

stem: A curator configures a Genie Agent and sorts the knowledge to enter. Which two items belong in the agent's general text instructions rather than in another instruction type? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The definition of "active customer", a filter that almost every revenue question uses, written as a sentence
A formatting rule: if the question gives no other specification, round all decimals to two places
The meaning of one ambiguous column such as `amt_2`, entered once as a general note for the whole agent
A multi-step comparison of cohort retention that needs several joins, described in prose for Genie to copy
The company's fiscal year starts on 1 February, so "FY26" means 1 February 2026 to 31 January 2027

stem: A Genie Agent's text instructions say "round all decimals to two places", but two of its example SQL queries round to whole numbers. Users see different rounding for similar questions and the curator wants consistent answers. What should the curator do?

choices.text: Delete every example query, because text instructions are the only source Genie treats as authoritative
Copy the rounding instruction into several table descriptions, so Genie reads it more often than it reads the examples
Write the rounding instruction again in capital letters, so it overrides the two example queries
Make the types agree, by changing the two example queries to round to two places

stem: Users ask a Genie Agent broad questions such as "how is sales performance?". Genie picks a time range and a channel on its own, and the figures are not what the users had in mind. The business wants Genie to ask for the missing details instead of guessing. Which configuration achieves this?

choices.text: Add the sentence "Be careful when answering sales questions" to the general instructions
Create a SQL expression that fixes the time range to the last 30 days and the channel to online for every sales question
Add a closing general instruction: if sales performance is asked without time range, channel or KPIs, ask first, with sample wording
Hide the date and channel columns so Genie cannot choose them without being told

stem: A new Genie Agent for support operations is shared with a wide audience. Users drift to topics the agent was never set up for (HR, finance) and get weak answers. The curator wants the first screen to steer users to what the agent handles well. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Configure sample questions for the supported tasks, phrased as users ask them and checked by the curator
Add the instruction "refuse every question that is not about support" and keep the unrelated tables in the agent
Leave sample questions empty and rely on users typing their own, because Genie answers questions on any topic equally well
Add every table of the support workspace to the agent so that any topic users raise has some data behind it

stem: A curator adds a general instruction saying to use `order_dt` for order dates. She then retests the same question in the chat where Genie had already answered wrongly several times, and the answer is still wrong. What should she do next?

choices.text: Retest in a new chat with a clean history, and if still wrong, add an example query that uses `order_dt`
Remove all text instructions and test again, since text instructions cannot influence which column is used
Restart the SQL warehouse attached to the agent, in case it holds the earlier wrong instruction in its cache
Rewrite the instruction in capital letters and add three paraphrases, so that Genie overrides the earlier wrong answers

stem: A support agent's prompt has 12 few-shot examples of about 150 tokens each. In an MLflow evaluation on a fixed dataset, correctness is 0.61 with no examples, 0.82 with three, 0.83 with six and 0.83 with twelve. Token cost matters. Which set should the team keep?

choices.text: None, since zero-shot is the cheapest configuration and examples only add cost
All twelve, since every added example scored at least as high as before
Six examples that are most similar to each other, so the output format is reinforced more strongly in every response
The three examples that produced the main gain, dropping the others whose marginal contribution is close to zero

stem: A returns-handling agent's prompt holds five few-shot examples, all clear-cut cases. Traces show it still fails on ambiguous requests, such as a refund request that is really an exchange. The team can add roughly the same number of example tokens. Which change is best?

choices.text: Replace the examples with full multi-turn conversations, so the model sees more context per example
Replace some examples with ones on the confusing boundary (refund versus exchange), showing the correct handling of each
Add ten more clear-cut examples of the same kind, since more examples of correct behavior generalize to ambiguous cases
Remove the examples and add a paragraph describing ambiguous cases, twice as long as the old examples

stem: A team keeps 10 few-shot examples in an extraction agent's prompt and must cut tokens without losing quality. It has an MLflow 3 evaluation dataset with scorers, and traces record the token count of every request. Which two steps let it decide which examples to keep? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Run the evaluation once with all 10 examples and drop the ones whose inputs look least like the dataset
Keep the examples with the most tokens, since long examples carry the most information per example
Re-run the same evaluation with each example removed in turn, and drop those whose removal leaves scores unchanged
Ask the model which examples it finds most useful, and drop those it ranks lowest in its own answer
Compare the score against the number of examples in several runs, and read per-request token cost from the traces

stem: A classification agent has 200 labeled examples across 15 intents, far too many for the prompt. A fixed set of five examples helps only some intents. The team wants help for every intent at a fixed token budget per request. Which design fits?

choices.text: Index the examples in AI Search and per request add only the few most similar to the incoming message
Put all 200 examples into an agent memory store and inject the store into the system prompt
Put all 200 examples in the prompt once and rely on the model's window to hold them for the whole conversation
Pick five examples at random for each request, so that over many requests every intent is shown to the model

stem: An email-drafting agent's prompt has three examples that all mention a customer called "Acme" and a refund of $45. Production outputs for unrelated customers keep mentioning Acme or $45. Which change corrects this?

choices.text: Move the three examples from the system prompt into the user turn, so the model treats them as the real request each time
Add "do not copy the examples" in capitals and keep the three examples exactly as they are
Vary names and amounts across examples, with marked placeholders for details that must not carry over
Repeat the same three examples twice more, so the format is learned strongly enough to stop the copying

stem: A 2,000-token system prompt works well except for refund questions, which are a few percent of requests: traces show the agent skipping the identity check that must precede any refund. The team wants the cheapest fix that is easy to maintain. Which is best?

choices.text: Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch with a new structure, so that all rules receive equal weight again, including refunds
Add one short, specific rule: before any refund, verify the customer's identity, and say which tool to call first
Paste the full 1,500-word refund policy into the prompt, so the agent has every detail at hand
Add ten worked refund examples at the end of the prompt, covering every refund situation in the policy

stem: A system prompt includes the line "Format dates correctly." Traces show the agent writing dates in several formats, which breaks a downstream parser. The team wants the fix that adds the fewest tokens. Which revision is best?

choices.text: Add three full sample dialogues in which every date is written correctly
Repeat "Format dates correctly" in capitals at the start, middle and end of the prompt
Keep the line and add an explanatory paragraph on why consistent dates matter to the downstream parser and reports
Replace it with a specific rule: "Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-11-09"

stem: After six incremental patches, a system prompt has overlapping rules and several "never do X" lines, and each new patch seems to break a different behavior. Which prompt-revision strategy is best?

choices.text: Freeze the prompt and cover the new failures by raising the reasoning effort for every request
Consolidate: merge overlapping rules, drop rules the traces show never matter, then re-run the same evaluation
Split the prompt into two system prompts and alternate between them on odd and even turns of the whole conversation
Keep appending each new fix at the end of the prompt, since the last lines are read most reliably

stem: Traces show an agent passing relative dates such as "next Friday" to its `get_shipments(ship_date STRING)` tool, which expects `YYYY-MM-DD`; the tool then fails. The team wants the lowest token cost and the easiest maintenance. Which two revisions fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Add five complete sample dialogues of correct tool calls to the system prompt, covering every date phrasing users have used
Turn on extended thinking for every request, so the model works out the format before each call
Copy the whole function signature and return schema into the system prompt as a second full description of the tool
Make the tool's failure message state the expected format and one valid example, so the agent corrects the call on a retry
Add a one-line rule to the system prompt: convert dates to `YYYY-MM-DD` before calling `get_shipments`, for example `2026-11-13`

stem: One agent serves 30 tenants. Each tenant has a few special rules, and the team currently keeps one growing system prompt with "if tenant is X" branches. The prompt is long, edits for one tenant have broken others, and every request carries rules for 29 tenants it does not need. Which revision fits best?

choices.text: Keep a short shared core prompt and insert only the current tenant's rules into it at request time
Keep all 30 tenants' branches in one prompt, but move them to the end so the model reads them last
Remove the tenant rules and let extended thinking infer what each tenant probably wants from the user's wording and tone
Make a full copy of the whole system prompt for each tenant and edit each copy separately

stem: A support agent's system prompt v1 is compared in MLflow 3 with a rewritten v2 that adds worked policy examples and roughly doubles the prompt's token count. Both versions ran through `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` on the same evaluation dataset with the same scorers. Correctness is 0.81 for v1 and 0.82 for v2, the Guidelines pass rate is identical, and the traces show several LLM calls per task. Should v2 replace v1?

choices.text: No, ever, because a longer system prompt always lowers accuracy by diluting the model's attention, regardless of what the scores show
Yes, because any gain on a quality scorer shows the extra instructions help, and added input tokens are cheap next to wrong answers
No, because a one-point gain is thin evidence while the doubled prompt is paid on every LLM call, so the extra tokens are not yet justified
Yes, once more judges are added, because only a larger scorer set can show whether a longer system prompt is better than a shorter one

stem: An MLflow 3 evaluation of an HR agent compares v1 with a v2 system prompt that adds a 300-token section on leave-policy exceptions. On the same dataset and scorers, the leave-policy slice (a minority of questions) rises from 0.52 to 0.88 Correctness, all other slices stay flat, `RetrievalGroundedness` and `Safety` do not regress, and the overall mean rises from 0.80 to 0.84. What does the experiment support?

choices.text: Defer v2 until production traffic is tested, because an evaluation dataset can never show whether prompt text changes behavior
Adopt v2, because the extra tokens target exactly the failing slice, the gain is large there, and nothing else regressed, so the cost buys a measured fix
Reject v2, because added instruction text is by definition context poisoning and should be removed whatever the scorers show
Reject v2, because the overall mean rose by only a few points and any prompt that adds tokens must lift every single slice to be acceptable on its own

stem: A team reports that its longer system prompt v2 "hurt quality": the MLflow experiment shows v1 at 0.84 Correctness and v2 at 0.71. Opening the runs, v1 was evaluated on the long-standing evaluation dataset, while v2 was evaluated on a newly built dataset of harder questions with an extra `Guidelines` scorer enabled. What is the right next step?

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples to v2 until its score exceeds 0.84, because the score gap is the thing to close
Accept the result and revert to v1, because a lower score on any evaluation dataset proves that the new prompt is worse than the old one was before it
Average the two runs' scores, because pooling them removes the difference between datasets and scorers
Re-run both versions on the same evaluation dataset with the same scorers, then compare, because the two runs are not comparable as recorded

stem: Two MLflow 3 evaluation runs on the same dataset and scorers compare a 150-token system prompt with a 900-token one that adds a style guide, a glossary and policy examples. Which TWO results most strongly support keeping the 900-token prompt? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Correctness on the cases the added policy examples cover rises substantially, with no drop on `RetrievalGroundedness` or `Safety`
The longer prompt's run has more registered scorers attached to it than the shorter prompt's run
The longer prompt reads as more thorough to the team when they review it, and a senior reviewer approved the wording of every section
A judge's rationale on one trace mentions the glossary, which shows the added text is being used by the model
Per-trace token usage in the spans stays within the cost and latency budget the application was designed for, after the increase

stem: A reviewer wants to estimate what v2's extra 400 system-prompt tokens cost per task in an agent whose MLflow 3 traces show six LLM spans per task. The system prompt is sent with every LLM call. Which estimate uses the experiment data correctly?

choices.text: Count only the 400 added tokens once per task, because the model reads the system prompt a single time at the start of the run
Read only the root span's output tokens, because input tokens in intermediate spans are billed to the tool and not to the model
Multiply the added prompt tokens by the LLM calls per task and confirm with per-span token usage, giving about 2,400 extra input tokens
Compare the character length of the two prompt versions, because token counts in traces are an unreliable measure of cost

stem: A Genie Agent over a billing table returns the wrong amount for "total revenue". The table has columns `amt_1`, `amt_2` and `amt_3` (gross invoiced, net of discounts, and refunded) and none has a Unity Catalog comment. Genie sometimes sums `amt_1` and sometimes `amt_3`. Which change has the largest effect on accuracy?

choices.text: Add the source system's full schema export to the agent as an additional table so Genie can look up the columns there
Enable entity matching on the three amount columns so Genie can read their stored values and infer the meaning from them
Add precise Unity Catalog column comments that state what each amount column holds, such as net of discounts and before refunds
Write a general text instruction that lists what every cryptic column means and tell Genie to prefer one of them for revenue

stem: A curator fixes confusing `customers.tier` semantics by editing the column description inside a Genie Agent. Genie now answers correctly, but a separate custom agent that queries the same table through a Unity Catalog SQL tool still misreads `tier`. Why, and what is the right fix for every consumer?

choices.text: Unity Catalog column comments cannot be edited after table creation, so the description has to be rebuilt by recreating the table with a new schema and reloading the data
Descriptions edited in a Genie Agent are scoped to that agent and do not change Unity Catalog, so the shared meaning belongs in the table's Unity Catalog column comment
Genie descriptions always override Unity Catalog, so the custom agent must be pointed at the Genie Agent to read the corrected description
The edit sits in a workspace cache, so the curator should wait for the refresh, after which both agents see the new text

stem: A Genie Agent over `orders` returns wrong date filters. The table has `order_dt` (the real order date), a legacy `order_date_legacy` still populated by an old job, and an `etl_batch_id` column. Other teams still read the legacy column, so it must stay in the Delta table. Which TWO changes most improve Genie's accuracy without breaking those teams? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Hide `order_date_legacy` and `etl_batch_id` in the Genie Agent, which removes them from its context but leaves the table intact
Apply a governed tag to the legacy columns, expecting Genie to skip any column carrying that tag when it writes SQL
Apply a column mask on the legacy columns in Unity Catalog so that every user, Genie included, gets masked values when reading them
Drop `order_date_legacy` and `etl_batch_id` from the Delta table so Genie cannot see them in Unity Catalog metadata
Add a precise description to `order_dt` stating it is the date the order was placed, plus synonyms such as order date and purchase date

stem: A Genie Agent over `tickets` has a `status` column that holds only the codes `P`, `R` and `C`. Entity matching is on and shows Genie all three values, yet "open tickets" returns only `status = 'P'` rows, while reopened tickets (`R`) also count as open. Which change fixes this?

choices.text: Add the synonym "open tickets" to the `status` column so that Genie treats the phrase as another name for that column in its queries
Refresh the stored values of the `status` column so that Genie re-reads the three codes and works out from the data which of them mean open
Add a general text instruction saying that open tickets have status P or R, and leave the codes themselves undocumented in the column
Describe the codes in the column description (P pending, R reopened, C closed) and define open tickets as a filter SQL expression on P or R

stem: A data steward accepted AI-generated comments for every column of a `contracts` table without editing them. Genie now confuses `owner_id` (the account manager's id) with the customer owner, because the generated comment says "unique identifier of the customer". What should the team do?

choices.text: Have an owner or user with MODIFY review and rewrite the comments for ambiguous columns using the business definition
Add a governed tag named account-manager to the column, because tags override comments when Genie reads metadata
Disable AI-generated comments for the workspace with the toggle, then keep the existing text as written
Regenerate the comments until the wording stabilizes, because repeated generation converges on the true business meaning

stem: A text instruction in a revenue Genie Agent says "For revenue by customer, use the view `fin.gold.v_order_customer`", but that view was never added under the agent's Sources. Genie keeps joining the raw tables that are attached, and answers vary between runs. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Repeat the instruction in stronger wording with the full view name several times, so that Genie queries the view despite its absence from Sources
Grant every agent user SELECT on the view, so that Genie can reach it through each user's own permissions when the instruction names it
Add the view to the agent's Sources and remove the raw tables that it replaces, so Genie chooses among objects that are really in its context
Paste the view's SQL into the instruction text, so that Genie can run the query itself without attaching the object to the agent

stem: A sales-operations Genie Agent must answer "what commission does rep X earn this quarter?". The calculation has tiered rates, clawbacks and an approved-exceptions lookup, cannot be written as a single parameterized query, and finance does not want the logic exposed or edited by Genie. Which trusted asset fits?

choices.text: A SQL expression that defines commission as a measure in the knowledge store for Genie to reuse in generated queries
A SQL function registered in Unity Catalog with rep and quarter as inputs, added to the agent, with EXECUTE granted to its users
A text instruction describing the tier table, clawback rules and exceptions lookup so Genie can rebuild the formula for each question
A parameterized example SQL query that contains the whole calculation and shows the rep and quarter as parameters

stem: Users of a regional sales Genie Agent repeatedly ask "What were sales in <region> for <quarter>?". Each answer should be a verified answer, not freshly generated SQL, and new regions and quarters appear every month. Which setup meets this?

choices.text: A general text instruction containing the SQL once, with a note telling Genie to substitute the region and quarter on each new question that arrives
One static example SQL query per region and quarter combination, each titled with its exact question
A knowledge-store join relationship between the sales and region tables so Genie derives the answer on its own
A parameterized example SQL query titled with the typical question, with typed region and quarter parameters whose comments describe the allowed values

stem: A finance schema contains `fin.silver.orders_raw_dupe` (a raw copy with duplicates), `fin.gold.v_order_customer` (a documented view that joins orders and customers), `fin.raw.invoice_pdfs` (a volume of scanned invoices), `fin.gold.mv_revenue` (a metric view that defines revenue, dimensions and aggregations) and `fin.silver.audit_events` (system audit rows). Which TWO objects should be curated into a Genie Agent for revenue analysis? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `fin.raw.invoice_pdfs`, so Genie can read the invoice documents for details
`fin.gold.mv_revenue`, the metric view that pre-defines revenue, its dimensions and its aggregations
`fin.silver.audit_events`, so Genie can explain who changed each figure
`fin.silver.orders_raw_dupe`, so Genie can fall back to the raw rows when views disagree
`fin.gold.v_order_customer`, the documented pre-joined view of orders and customers

stem: A Genie Agent for order analytics lists both `sales.orders` and `sales.orders_v1`. The old table was replaced last year and is flagged deprecated, but its numbers differ slightly and Genie sometimes queries it, producing inconsistent answers between sessions. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Add a text instruction telling Genie never to use `orders_v1` and leave the table in the agent's data objects
Hide every column of `orders_v1` in the agent but keep the table listed in its data objects, so that existing example queries still reference it
Remove `orders_v1` from the agent's data objects and tag it deprecated with `system.certification_status`
Rename `orders_v1` to `orders_v1_old` in Unity Catalog so the new name reduces how often Genie selects it

stem: A parts-lookup agent uses an AI Search index over product manuals. Questions such as "torque spec for part NX-4471-B" retrieve chunks about other parts, because the index uses the default approximate-nearest-neighbor query type. Natural-language questions work well. Which change fixes the identifier failures with the least extra context?

choices.text: Replace the embedding model with a larger one, since larger embeddings represent identifiers exactly
Re-chunk the manuals into much smaller pieces so each chunk carries a single part number
Raise `num_results` so that the exact part number appears somewhere among a much larger set of returned chunks
Change the query type to hybrid so keyword matching on the exact part number complements semantic similarity

stem: In a trace, the AI Search retrieval span returns the right chunk, but at rank seven of ten, and the agent answers from the three chunks at the top, which are loosely related. Raising `num_results` further would add more tokens. Which change addresses the ranking directly?

choices.text: Enable the AI Search reranker on the query, listing the relevant text columns in `columns_to_rerank`, and pass only the top few reranked chunks
Re-embed the corpus with heavy chunk overlap so that neighboring chunks repeat the same relevant text and any one of them can rank higher
Rewrite the retriever tool description so the agent calls the tool more often per question
Increase `num_results` again so that the right chunk is always included in what the model reads

stem: An agent queries a standard-endpoint AI Search index with `filters={"published_year": ">= 2024"}` to keep only recent policies. The retrieval span shows no matching documents and the agent answers without retrieved context, although many 2025 policies exist. `published_year` is an indexed integer column. What is the cause and fix?

choices.text: Numeric columns cannot be filtered at all, so store the year as text in a second column and filter that column with `LIKE`
Filters are applied only after reranking, so enable the reranker first so that the range test has ranked chunks to work on
With no operator in the key, a filter is an exact-match test, so put the operator in the key, as in `{"published_year >=": 2024}`
Range filters work only with the hybrid query type, so switch the query from the default ANN type and keep the same filter

stem: A customer-help agent retrieves from a large product-manual index. Traces show that the right chunk usually appears in the top candidates, but the model also receives many chunks from other product lines, and answers sometimes cite the wrong product. The team wants higher precision without increasing the number of chunks in the prompt. Which TWO changes achieve this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Turn off hybrid search so that only semantic similarity ranks results and keywords stop pulling in other products
Apply a metadata filter on the indexed `product_line` column when the product is known or can be extracted from the question
Switch to a much larger chunk size so that every result carries more text from a single manual
Raise `num_results` to the largest practical value so that the correct chunk is nearly always included
Use the reranker on a wider candidate set, then pass only the top few reranked chunks to the model

stem: An agent's first retrieval after a quiet period times out, and in that run the agent answers from general knowledge with no retrieved context; the next retrievals succeed. The index uses a Databricks-computed embedding model served from a model serving endpoint that has the default scale-to-zero selection. What is the likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The embedding endpoint scaled to zero and needs minutes to warm up, so turn off scale to zero for the endpoint that serves the index
The reranker is cold, so remove `columns_to_rerank` from the first call and add it again for later calls
The index sync mode is triggered, so switch to continuous sync to prevent the first query from timing out
The index has too many synced columns, so reduce `columns_to_sync` to the text column alone to speed up the first call after idle time

stem: Thousands of PDF contracts land in a Unity Catalog volume. They contain tables and numbered clauses, and the agent must cite the contract and page it used. Which pipeline design supplies useful chunks to the agent's context?

choices.text: Store the PDF bytes in a Delta table column and embed that binary column directly, since the index accepts columns of any type for embedding
Extract raw text page by page, concatenate each file into one string, embed each whole file, and return the files
Leave the PDFs in the volume and give the agent a tool that reads and returns a whole PDF each time it is asked
Parse the PDFs keeping tables, chunk by clause, store chunks with source path and page in a Delta table, and index it for a retriever tool

stem: An agent uses two tools, `list_volume_files` and `read_volume_file`, to read runbooks from a Unity Catalog volume with the Databricks SDK Files API. The trace shows a permission-denied error on `list_volume_files`. The agent runs as a service principal. Which grants are needed on the volume's catalog, schema and volume?

choices.text: `SELECT` on the catalog and `MODIFY` on the schema so the agent can read tables in the volume
`WRITE VOLUME` and `CREATE VOLUME`, since reading a file requires write access to the volume
`USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema and `READ VOLUME` on the volume
`ALL PRIVILEGES` on the catalog, because volume reads are covered only by full ownership

stem: A retriever tool over an AI Search index returns, for every result, the chunk text plus twenty metadata columns: ingestion timestamps, content hashes, a parse-debug blob and the full parsed JSON. Traces show retrieval results are several times larger than the chunks themselves, and answers drift. The agent only needs the text and the source path. What is the best change?

choices.text: Limit the tool's returned `columns` to the chunk text and source path, and keep `num_results` modest
Move to a model with a larger context window, so that the extra metadata no longer matters
Instruct the model in the system prompt to ignore every column except the text and the source path
Delete the metadata columns from the Delta table so the index cannot return them or filter on them

stem: A policy PDF in a Unity Catalog volume is replaced by a revised version. After the nightly pipeline reprocesses it, the agent's answers mix the old and the revised rules, and the trace shows chunks from both versions in the retrieval results. The chunk table is append-only and keyed by chunk id. What should change in the pipeline?

choices.text: Increase the reranker's candidate count so that the newer chunks outrank the older chunks of the same policy
Lower `num_results` to one, so that only the single best-ranked chunk is returned for each question and the conflict cannot reach the model
Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to prefer the newer version whenever two chunks conflict
On reprocessing, replace all chunks keyed to the file's source path (MERGE or delete then insert), and let the Delta Sync index pick up the change

stem: An operations agent needs eight short Markdown runbooks stored in a Unity Catalog volume. Each runbook must be read in full to be safe to follow, the set changes occasionally, and nobody wants an indexing pipeline for it. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Build a parse, chunk, embed and Delta Sync index pipeline over the runbooks, and return the top chunks for each question
Give the agent list and read tools over the volume so it opens only the runbook it needs, in full, when a task calls for it
Split the runbooks into one row per sentence in a Delta table and index it with hybrid search, returning the best sentences
Paste all eight runbooks into the system prompt so every call includes the complete set

stem: A coding assistant answers questions from a Python repository stored in a Unity Catalog volume. The pipeline cuts every file into pieces of 60 lines, and traces show retrieved chunks that start inside a function body or hold the end of one function and the start of the next, so the model cannot tell which function a snippet belongs to. Which chunking change fits the structure of source code?

choices.text: Embed each whole source file as one chunk, so every function stays together with its neighbors and no definition is ever cut in a result
Cut every 30 lines instead of 60, so that fewer functions are split across two chunks and each chunk holds less unrelated code
Split on blank lines and comment lines, so that every block of code becomes a small chunk of its own and statements stay on separate chunks
Split on function and class definitions so each one stays whole, and keep the file path and enclosing class or function name with the chunk

stem: A policy agent embeds 400-token body chunks. Before embedding, the pipeline prepends a 150-token header (document summary, title, section path) to each body. The embedding model's documented maximum input is 512 tokens. Questions about the last part of each body are never retrieved, although the text is in the Delta table, while questions about the first paragraphs work. What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Keep header plus body within the embedding model's maximum input, for example by cutting the body to about 350 tokens, or choose a model that accepts longer input
Raise the chunk overlap to 25% so that late sentences of one chunk are also repeated at the start of the next chunk, where they fit within the limit
Raise `num_results` so that the chunks holding the late content come back, even though their embedded vectors reflect only the header and the early body
Switch the generation model to one with a larger context window, so that the full chunks can be read in whole by the agent once they are returned

stem: An agent answers questions over 20-page quarterly reports chunked by section. Narrow questions such as "What was churn in the EMEA segment?" work well. Broad questions such as "Summarize the main risks in the Q3 report" retrieve a few arbitrary risk-related sections and the answer misses most of the report. Which change to the index suits both query types?

choices.text: Replace the section chunks by one chunk per sentence, since a very small unit makes broad questions find every sentence about risks
Raise the section chunk size to a whole report, since this alone makes the narrow questions work as well as before for each segment
Add one summary chunk per report, generated at ingestion and linked to the report by an id, next to the existing section chunks
Raise `num_results` to 40 so that most of the sections of the report are returned for every question, narrow ones included, to cover all risks

stem: A team must choose the chunk size for a new support agent before indexing 100,000 articles. Which TWO inputs should drive the choice? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The response speed of the chat model, because chunk size must match how fast the model can write the answer
Where the answers to typical user questions sit in the articles (a sentence, a section or several sections), from sampled questions
The number of articles in the corpus, because a larger corpus always needs a larger chunk size to keep the index small
The file extension of each article alone, because every format has one fixed chunk size that works well for all content
The maximum input length of the chosen embedding model, which caps the tokens that can be represented in one vector

stem: After a corpus update, an agent's retriever returns 4 chunks per question, each a full 12-page chapter. The trace shows retrieval results that account for most of the prompt, and the answer is usually one sentence located in a single subsection. Answers often cite the right chapter but include unrelated details from other subsections. What should change in the pipeline?

choices.text: Chunk by subsection (or paragraph groups) into smaller, semantically coherent chunks and keep the chapter title as metadata
Increase `num_results` to ten so that more of the chapters containing the answer are returned and the model has a better chance of finding the sentence
Use a reranker on the chapter-sized chunks, since reranking will remove the unrelated subsections from inside each chunk
Add a system prompt rule telling the model to ignore the parts of each chapter that are not relevant to the question

stem: A refund agent receives "Refund order 8841, the blender arrived broken" from a signed-in customer. The team wants to assemble the minimum context for the model to scope and complete this task. Which set of context elements is the best fit?

choices.text: Only the customer's message, since the model can infer the policy, the order status and the tool to call from the wording alone
The full conversation history of all customers with the same product, so the agent can see how earlier refunds were handled
The complete policy handbook, every tool the company has registered, and the customer's lifetime order list in case any of them is needed
The task instruction with refund policy rules, the order 8841 record and status, the customer's identity, and the refund tool definition

stem: A scheduling agent must book a meeting after the user says, "Set up 30 minutes with Priya next Tuesday afternoon, my time zone." Which TWO context elements does the agent specifically need to scope and execute this task? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A long description of the company's org chart, so the agent knows the reporting line of everybody in the company
The booking tool's definition with its parameter schema, plus Priya's availability for the requested window
The full text of the company's meeting etiquette handbook, in case any etiquette rule might be relevant
The calendar history of every employee for the past year, so the agent can learn when people usually accept meetings
The user's time zone and today's date, supplied by the application at request time so "next Tuesday" resolves correctly

stem: A sales agent is asked, "How is my region doing this quarter?" It returns figures for the wrong quarter and for the wrong region on different days. The context holds the system prompt, the question and a tool that queries a revenue table by region and period. Nothing else about the session is passed in. Which missing context element best fixes this?

choices.text: A longer list of example questions with answers, so that the model learns to guess the likeliest region and period from the wording alone
The full revenue table pasted into the prompt, so that the model can work out the region and the quarter for itself
Runtime session context supplied by the application: the user's region from their profile and the current date or fiscal quarter
A rule that the agent should always ask the user to restate the region and the period before every single question

stem: An HR benefits agent receives the question "Can I sue my manager for this review?" and starts giving legal-sounding advice. The agent's context contains the benefits documents and a system prompt that says only "You are a helpful HR assistant." Which missing context element most directly fixes the failure?

choices.text: A larger set of benefits documents, so that the agent has more material to consider when it forms its answer
An explicit scope statement: benefits questions are covered, legal advice is not, and out-of-scope requests are routed to HR or legal
A prompt telling the model to think step by step before every answer, so that it analyses each incoming question more carefully and thoroughly
Metadata describing the length of each benefits document, so the agent can pick shorter documents first

stem: A report-drafting agent produces accurate figures from its retrieved sources, but each draft uses a different layout, and downstream automation that parses the drafts fails. The context holds the user request, the source passages and a prompt saying "write a quarterly summary". Which missing element should be added?

choices.text: More source passages per request, since accurate content implies that the layout will converge once enough sources are included
A second model call that re-reads the draft and rewrites it, without telling the second call which layout is expected
The full history of earlier drafts, so the model infers the layout from whichever earlier drafts happen to be in the window
An output specification: the required sections, a template or schema for the draft, and an example of the expected format

stem: A product-FAQ chatbot answers customers from a single documentation index. Every question needs documentation to answer correctly, the application cannot tolerate an answer given without retrieval, and the team wants predictable latency with one model call per question. Which retrieval pattern fits?

choices.text: Retrieval only after the model has produced a first answer, to check that answer against the index and rewrite it if necessary
Just-in-time agentic retrieval, where the model decides on each turn whether to call the search tool and may call it repeatedly while it works
Pre-inference retrieval: the application queries the index with the user's question before the model call and places the top chunks in the prompt
No retrieval, with the full documentation placed in the system prompt so every call already holds everything it could need

stem: A coding-assistant agent works across a large repository, a wiki, a ticket system and release notes. A typical task needs two or three files that cannot be known in advance, and the right next lookup depends on what the previous lookup found. Which retrieval pattern fits best?

choices.text: Just-in-time agentic retrieval: give the agent search and read tools so it fetches what it needs, step by step, using what each result reveals
A fixed query formed from the first message, run once before inference, with the agent not allowed to search again
Pre-inference retrieval of the top chunks from all four sources for each user message, placed in the prompt before the first model call and the first reasoning step
Loading the whole repository and wiki into the context at the start so that every possible lookup is already available

stem: A compliance agent uses just-in-time retrieval with a policy retriever tool. Evaluation traces show that on about a fifth of questions the agent answers from its general knowledge without calling the retriever, and `RetrievalGroundedness` cannot be computed for those runs. Policy citations are mandatory for every answer. What is the most robust change?

choices.text: Rewrite the system prompt in capital letters, telling the model to always search, and keep the retriever as an optional tool
Increase the number of results per call so that, when the agent does search, it returns more material to cite
Move policy retrieval to pre-inference, so the application always queries the index and injects the chunks before the model call
Add a second retriever tool over the same index with a different name, so the agent has more chances to choose one

stem: Which TWO statements describe trade-offs of just-in-time agentic retrieval compared with pre-inference retrieval? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It guarantees that retrieval runs on every single request, because the model always calls a retriever whenever one is registered with it
Each retrieval is an additional tool call and model round trip, so latency and token use can rise on questions that need several lookups
It makes the prompt larger in every case, because all candidate chunks are loaded before the first model call
It removes the need for a good tool name and description, since the model discovers the right source by itself
The agent can reformulate its query, or search another source, after reading earlier results, which suits questions that need follow-ups

stem: A telecom support agent always needs the caller's plan, contract end date and open case number, which sit in one governed table and are looked up by customer id. It also needs knowledge articles, but which article depends on the diagnosis the agent reaches while talking with the caller. Which design fits best?

choices.text: Inject the three account fields before inference from a keyed lookup, and expose an AI Search retriever tool so the agent fetches articles just in time
Expose both the account lookup and the article search as tools, so that the agent decides every time what to fetch, including the account fields
Place all knowledge articles and all account tables in the system prompt, because mixing both types in one place keeps the design simple
Run pre-inference retrieval of the top articles for the caller's first sentence, and leave out the account fields until the caller asks

stem: An MLflow 3 evaluation of a product agent with ground-truth expectations reports high `RetrievalRelevance` (retrieved chunks are on topic), low `RetrievalSufficiency`, and low Correctness on warranty questions. The trace shows the retrieval span returns on-topic marketing pages, and Unity Catalog metadata shows that the approved warranty terms table is not part of the index's source table. Which failure mode and governance action fit?

choices.text: Distraction by oversized chunks; split the marketing pages into smaller chunks, since size is the cause of the low sufficiency
Stale source; deprecate the marketing pages in Unity Catalog, because stale content is what makes sufficiency fall below relevance
Ranking failure; enable the reranker, because the right text is already in the index and only needs a better position
Missing authoritative source; have the data steward add the approved warranty terms to the governed corpus that the index syncs from

stem: Evaluation of a pricing agent shows correct-looking but outdated answers. In the retrieval spans, the top chunks come from a table called `pricing.archive.price_list_2023`, whose Unity Catalog `system.certification_status` is `deprecated`, while the current `pricing.gold.price_list` is `certified` and is also in the index. Which action resolves the failure?

choices.text: Remove the deprecated archive from the index source (for example by syncing the index from a materialized view over certified assets) and re-sync
Increase the reranker's candidate pool so that the certified table has more chances to outrank the archive
Delete the evaluation rows that expose the outdated answers so the aggregate scores improve and the failing slice disappears from the report
Add a prompt rule telling the agent to prefer chunks that look recent, so that dates in the text decide the winner

stem: Traces for an onboarding agent show retrieval spans citing files under `/Volumes/hr/scratch/drafts/`, where employees save personal notes. `RetrievalRelevance` is low for those spans, and answers sometimes contradict the HR handbook. The agent's service principal holds `READ VOLUME` on the whole `hr` catalog's volumes. Which governance action addresses the cause?

choices.text: Ask employees to stop saving notes in the drafts volume, because a naming convention on personal files is enough to protect the agent
Lower the number of results per query so that the draft files rarely fall within the returned results
Tell the model in the system prompt that files under drafts are unreliable, and keep the broad read grant in place
Limit the service principal's read access to the curated handbook volume, so the drafts volume is no longer a possible source

stem: A shared HR assistant queries one AI Search index with its app's service principal for every employee. The index is synced from a table that holds both employee-handbook text and compensation-band documents. Review of a trace shows that a regular employee received chunks from compensation bands that only the HR team may see. Retrieval quality scores are good. Which governance change resolves this at its source?

choices.text: Add a system prompt rule that forbids the assistant from ever revealing compensation data to people who are not on the HR team, wherever it appears
Build the assistant's index only from the employee-facing handbook table, and keep compensation bands in a separate index that only the HR group can query
Increase the reranker's strictness so that compensation chunks are ranked lower for questions that are not about pay or salary bands in any way
Split the compensation bands into smaller chunks so that each chunk contains too little text to identify a role or a person in the results

stem: A procurement agent sometimes gives conflicting answers. Retrieval spans show two supplier-policy documents in different Unity Catalog volumes: `/Volumes/proc/policy/v2024/` and `/Volumes/proc/legal/copy_of_policy/`. Both are indexed, neither carries a certification status, and no steward is recorded for either. Which governance action resolves the conflict at its source?

choices.text: Raise the retrieval result count so that both versions always appear and the model can pick whichever it judges to be more recent
Rewrite the system prompt to say that when sources disagree the agent should refuse to answer the procurement question
Designate one owner and one authoritative version, certify it, deprecate the other, and rebuild the index from the certified source only
Fine-tune the generation model on the latest policy text so that it overrides whatever retrieval returns about suppliers

stem: A bank is preparing a customer-policy agent for deployment. Policy documents live in many Unity Catalog volumes, some drafts, some archived. Compliance requires that the agent cite only approved policy. Which pre-deployment strategy achieves this?

choices.text: Index everything but rank approved policy higher by boosting the words "approved" and "official" in each query
Create a curated schema holding only approved policy, certify its assets, index only that source, and grant the agent access to it alone
Put every policy volume into one AI Search index and ask the agent to cite the most official-looking source in each answer it gives
Rely on the evaluation set alone: if the answers score well on correctness, the sources must have been approved ones

stem: A release checklist for a retrieval agent is being drafted. Which TWO checks, performed before deployment, best confirm that retrieval is restricted to authoritative sources? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Confirm that the agent's average response latency stays below the team's target on every query in the evaluation set
Compare the number of indexed chunks with the previous release and accept the release if the count has grown since the last deployment
Run the evaluation set with tracing and inspect the source path in each retrieval span to confirm every cited document is approved
Check that the system prompt includes the sentence "only use official documents" in a prominent position
Review the index's source tables and volumes in Unity Catalog, confirming that each has an owner and a `certified` status, and that no deprecated or draft asset feeds the index

stem: A company keeps all finance documents in one catalog. To deploy a budget-planning agent safely, an engineer proposes granting its service principal `SELECT` and `READ VOLUME` on the whole catalog "so it never hits a permission error". Only about a tenth of the catalog is approved planning material. What is the better strategy?

choices.text: Keep the broad grant, since permission errors in production cause outages, and tell the prompt to avoid the unapproved folders and schemas
Grant access to the whole catalog for the test phase only and remove it after launch, because testing needs full visibility to find every gap in the corpus
Give the agent a user's personal credentials so the access stays with a human who understands which folders are approved
Grant the service principal access only to the approved planning schema and volume (and the AI Search index built from them), using a dedicated principal for this agent

stem: A data steward certified the approved `claims.gold` tables, and the team assumed that the claims agent would therefore retrieve only from certified data. A trace shows the agent returning rows from `claims.staging.raw_claims`, which is uncertified, because the agent's service principal has `SELECT` on the whole `claims` catalog. What is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: The tag only labels assets and does not restrict reads, so the grants and the data sources the agent uses must be limited to certified assets
The tag only takes effect once the agent's prompt mentions the certification status in its instructions and names the tag key
Certification has failed, and the steward should reapply the tag to the staging table so that Unity Catalog starts to block reads of it
Unity Catalog will block reads of uncertified tables once a propagation delay passes, so the staging reads should stop

stem: In a knowledge-management workspace the ASSIGN permission on the `system.certification_status` governed tag was granted to all account users, and several teams have certified their own working copies. The governance lead wants "certified" to mean "approved by data stewards" so the agent's retrieval corpus can be built from certified assets only. Which control gives the tag that meaning?
