choices.text: Add a rule to the agent prompt that rejects chunks from tables whose owners are not on the stewards list
Document in the team wiki that only stewards should certify assets, and review the tags once a year
Restrict the ASSIGN permission on the `system.certification_status` governed tag to the stewards group
Rename the working-copy tables with a `_draft` suffix so that engineers recognise them as unapproved

stem: A travel agent is built on LangGraph, and the framework's own checkpointer already persists the graph state of each chat, so a chat resumes after a restart. Travelers now complain that a seat preference stated in one chat is unknown in the next chat. What should the team add?

choices.text: Append a growing list of every traveler's stated preferences to the shared system prompt that all the chats receive
Add agent memory for durable preferences recalled by semantic search, and keep the checkpointer for in-chat state
Replace the checkpointer's persisted graph state with agent memory so that no per-chat state is stored by the agent at all
Move the checkpointer state into an agent session store, since a session carries the traveler's state into every later chat

stem: A planning agent crashes midway through a long conversation and restarts. Its memory store still holds the user's stable preferences, but after the restart the agent has lost the tool calls and intermediate results it had gathered in this conversation. Which memory strategy closes the gap?

choices.text: Persist the interaction's working state in an agent session and read it at the start of each turn so the conversation resumes
Run the memory pipeline more often so every tool result becomes a long-term memory entry the moment it is produced
Remove the memory store and keep all preferences in the conversation, so that one component holds all state
Store the intermediate results as embeddings in the memory store and rely on semantic search to rebuild the plan order

stem: A travel agent already keeps each chat in a session store. The team wants it to act on the following needs. Which TWO needs require long-term memory rather than session history? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Reusing the departure city the user typed a minute ago while refining the same search
Keeping the result of the flight search that was run two turns ago in the same conversation
Showing the three most recent messages again after the user scrolls back up in the open chat
Remembering that this traveler always wants an aisle seat and a vegetarian meal when booking in any later trip
Recalling that last spring the traveler rejected a particular airline because of a baggage dispute

stem: A team lead reads the Databricks memory research mapping and asks which component plays which role. Which statement matches how the docs map the session store, the memory store and the memory pipeline?

choices.text: Both stores hold episodic memory, and the pipeline fine-tunes the model on them during an offline step so that sessions are no longer needed
The session store holds derived memory, the memory store holds the raw record, and the pipeline replays that record into every new prompt
The session store holds episodic memory, the raw record of each session; the memory store holds derived memory; the pipeline distills the first into the second
The session store holds derived memory, the memory store holds episodic memory, and the pipeline copies the episodic records back into sessions

stem: A research agent works on one very long task in a single conversation. Its trace shows the context filling up with early tool outputs, and a teammate proposes adding a cross-user long-term memory store to fix it. Why is that the wrong memory strategy, and what fits better?

choices.text: Long-term memory is only for system prompts, so the earlier tool outputs should be moved into the system prompt
The problem is in-interaction state growth, so trim or compact the session's context and keep large results outside the window
Long-term memory cannot be searched semantically, so the agent should use keyword lookups of its earlier tool outputs instead
Memory stores are deleted whenever a session ends, so nothing could be recalled for the remainder of the task

stem: A compliance team wants a complete record of every interaction an assistant had, available for replay, and also wants the assistant to personalize answers from what it learned about each customer. Which store layout matches these two information needs?

choices.text: Keep the full replayable records in the session store and the distilled customer facts in the memory store, fed by a memory pipeline
Keep replayable records in the memory store and distilled facts in the system prompt, rewritten whenever a customer returns
Keep both needs in the session store, and let the agent search old transcripts each time it personalizes an answer
Keep both needs in one memory store, since distilled facts and replayable records have the same scope

stem: An agent runs a multi-day vendor onboarding workflow across many job runs. It tracks which of the checklist steps are done in a scratchpad it writes into its own context. After a restart and after a compaction, the checklist is gone and finished steps are repeated. What should the team change?

choices.text: Increase the maximum output length so the scratchpad can hold the full checklist history in each response
Ask the model to keep a running summary of the checklist at the end of every reply so compaction preserves it
Write the steps to a longer scratchpad in the system prompt so that the checklist is always at the top of the window
Store task and step status in a Delta table that the agent reads and updates, and load only the rows it needs each step

stem: A math tutoring agent solves a problem in one turn. It writes a three-line plan, computes two intermediate values, and then answers in the same turn. Nothing is needed after the turn ends. Which approach to the intermediate state is best?

choices.text: Create a Delta state table with a row per intermediate value so the work is auditable by future runs
Write the values to a Lakebase table and read them back at the start of the next unrelated conversation
Keep the plan and values in an in-context scratchpad for the turn because nothing needs to outlive it
Save the plan to the agent memory store as a durable fact so the tutor can reuse it for other students

stem: Several agents work in parallel on one claims case: an intake agent, a document agent and a fraud agent. They each need to see which sub-tasks others finished, and an auditor must later query who did what and when. Which TWO designs meet these needs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Record each agent's actions as rows with timestamps and agent ids in that same Delta table so auditors can query them with SQL
Hold sub-task status only in the memory store as semantically searchable facts about the case
Have each agent keep its own scratchpad and exchange summaries of it by pasting them into the next agent's prompt
Rely on the orchestrator's context window to hold all sub-task status and reconstruct the audit trail from its trace
Store sub-task state in a shared Delta table keyed by case and sub-task, which every agent reads and updates

stem: A coding agent keeps appending a note to its scratchpad after every tool call. By step forty, the trace shows the scratchpad filling the window with notes about steps that finished long ago, and the agent starts misreading the current step. What change best fits?

choices.text: Tell the agent to write shorter notes from now on, and keep all of them in the scratchpad
Duplicate the scratchpad into the system prompt so that the current step is read twice
Reformat the notes in a different markup style so that the important ones are marked as high priority in the window
Move the finished steps into a Delta state table and keep in the window only the active step and the notes it needs

stem: A data-quality agent compares thousands of rows across tables and must track a counter, a list of failed checks and the last row processed. Runs can be interrupted and resumed hours later by a different worker. Which approach is the most reliable?

choices.text: Ask the model to track the counter and failed checks in its scratchpad and recompute them whenever the run resumes
Store the counter, failed checks and last processed position in a Delta state table and have each resumed run read them before continuing
Print the counter and failed checks into the final answer so the next worker can copy them from the previous message
Put the failed-check list in the memory store as a semantically searchable fact and fetch it by similarity when the run resumes

stem: A billing agent stores each customer's facts as rows in Lakebase Postgres. A user asks, "What is my current plan tier?" The tier is a single column on the customer row identified by the authenticated customer id. Which retrieval approach fits?

choices.text: Run a hybrid keyword and similarity search over the whole table and take the top-ranked row
A structured SQL query that filters the row by customer id and selects the tier column
Embed all customer rows into an index and run a similarity search with the question text
Ask the model to guess the tier from the previous conversation summary and verify it later

stem: A wellness agent stores free-text notes from earlier chats. A user now says, "Remember that thing we talked about when I was stressed about my sister's wedding?" No note contains the words "stressed" or "wedding"; they say "anxious about family event." Which retrieval approach should the agent use over the stored notes?

choices.text: A structured query ordered by note timestamp, returning the latest note
A SQL equality filter on the word "wedding" in the notes column
A SQL LIKE pattern for "stressed" so the agent can match notes containing the same word
Semantic search over embeddings of the notes, ranked by meaning

stem: An account agent can look up memory two ways: a structured SQL query on Lakebase tables, or semantic search over note text. Which TWO lookups should use the structured query? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Count how many support cases for this account were closed during the current quarter
Find notes that resemble how an unhappy customer described a recurring outage in their own words
Recall earlier chats where the user hinted at being worried about budget without stating a number
Surface notes semantically close to a vague phrase such as "the thing about my shipment"
Return the account's current preferred_language value stored as a column on the customer row

stem: An agent keeps memory about product orders, with notes such as "replacement for XK-9921-B shipped late". When a user asks about order "XK-9921-B", pure embedding search ranks notes about other products with similar-sounding descriptions above the exact identifier match. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Remove identifiers from the notes before embedding so the search focuses on meaning only
Increase the embedding dimension of the notes so identifiers become more distinct in vector space
Use hybrid keyword-similarity search so exact identifier matches are scored alongside semantic matches
Lower the number of results returned to one so the first similarity hit is always the right one

stem: A shared agent stores memories for many customers. A semantic search for "my last complaint" returns a close match that belongs to a different customer, and the trace shows the other customer's note in the prompt. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Raise the similarity threshold so that only near-identical notes are returned for any query
Switch to a larger embedding model so that notes from different customers become easier to tell apart by meaning
Apply a customer id filter as a predicate on the search, so only that customer's notes are candidates
Add instructions to the system prompt telling the model to ignore notes that mention other customers

stem: A team runs three memory-injection configurations through the same evaluation dataset and judges, five MLflow runs each, and records correctness: config A mean 0.84 (range 0.62 to 0.95), config B mean 0.81 (range 0.78 to 0.84), config C mean 0.70 (range 0.69 to 0.71). Which configuration is the most stable choice for production?

choices.text: Config C, because its range is the narrowest and consistency matters more than quality
Config A, because it reached the highest single score and can be tuned to match it every time
Config A, because mean correctness is the only quantity that matters when comparing runs
Config B, because its results stay in a narrow range at a high level across repeated runs

stem: A team evaluates a memory-enabled agent with MLflow 3 on 80 single-turn questions, each answerable from the question text alone, once with memory injection off and once on. Correctness is 0.83 in both runs, and the team concludes that memory adds nothing. What is wrong with this conclusion and what is the fix?

choices.text: Memory should be judged on latency only, so drop the quality scorers and compare the duration of the traces for both runs
The dataset never needs earlier-conversation facts, so add rows that depend on prior chats, with expectations, and rerun both configurations
The judge is too lenient, so replace correctness with a stricter groundedness judge and score the same single-turn questions again
Two runs are too few, so repeat each configuration ten times and base the decision on the larger mean of the same dataset

stem: Two memory configurations score the same mean correctness in MLflow. Config X injects a short summary of the user's history; config Y injects the five most recent raw transcript snippets. The team must decide which to ship and can inspect the evaluation traces. Which evidence best breaks the tie?

choices.text: Compare per-trace judge feedback on the lowest-scoring rows and the tokens each configuration put into the context
Pick config Y because longer injected text always indicates a richer memory and therefore produces better answers for users
Pick whichever configuration was evaluated first because earlier runs are less likely to have been tuned
Average the two configurations' scores together so a joint value represents both memories

stem: Version v1 and version v2 of a memory-enabled agent were run through `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` on the same dataset. A reviewer wants to see exactly how the memory change altered the answer to one request. Which TWO steps in the MLflow UI do that? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Delete the v1 run so that the UI shows only the v2 traces as the baseline that is left for the dataset
Open only the v2 run's trace list and rely on the reviewer's recollection of what the v1 answer looked like
Click the request identifier in the comparison to open the full trace of that request from each selected run
Compare the two runs' experiment-level average scores and treat any gap as the explanation for that request
Check the boxes for both runs in Evaluation runs and choose Compare from the Actions drop-down menu

stem: Across repeated MLflow evaluation runs, config P injects ten memory items per request and config Q injects three. Both reach about the same correctness and groundedness, but P's traces show far larger inputs and slower responses. Which configuration is the better context choice?

choices.text: Config P, because response time is not a property of the context configuration
Config P, because injecting more items is safer even if correctness does not improve
Neither, because equal scores mean that the memory injection has no effect on quality and should be removed entirely
Config Q, because it reaches the same quality with a leaner context and less attention budget

stem: A concierge agent always needs the traveler's name, home airport, language and loyalty tier for every request, and these fields are stable columns on one Lakebase row. Which retrieval approach to this memory is best?

choices.text: Retrieve the profile only after the model replies, then append it to the answer text
Static retrieval: query the profile row before the model call and place the small fixed block in the prompt every time
Dynamic retrieval only: give the model a tool and let it decide whether to look up the profile on each request
Run a semantic search over the whole memory store on each request and take whatever ranks highest

stem: A voice assistant has a strict latency budget. Traces show that on nearly every call the agent first calls a memory lookup tool that runs the same query for the caller's next appointment (one small Lakebase row) and only then answers. The tool round trip is the slowest step. What is the best change?

choices.text: Run that fixed appointment query before the model call and place the row in the prompt; keep the tool for rare memories
Make the tool return every stored memory for the caller so that a second lookup is never needed later
Cache the model's final answers per caller for a day so that repeated calls skip memory and retrieval
Keep the lookup tool as it is and lengthen its description so that the model calls it with less hesitation

stem: A team moves an agent from static memory injection to a dynamic memory lookup tool on Lakebase. Which TWO trade-offs should they expect? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Context size no longer varies, because the tool returns the same number of tokens for every question
Each lookup adds a tool-call round trip, so requests that use memory take longer than a preloaded block
Every relevant memory is now guaranteed to enter the context because the model always calls the tool
Tool descriptions are no longer needed because the model automatically knows what is in the memory store
The agent may skip the lookup or phrase a poor query, which can leave relevant memories out of the context

stem: A banking assistant has a small set of facts it needs on every turn (customer segment, preferred channel) and a large history of past service notes that matter only occasionally. Which retrieval design best balances predictability and token cost?

choices.text: Retrieve both sets statically before every model call so that nothing depends on the model's decisions
Retrieve both sets dynamically so that the model decides about the segment and channel as well
Skip retrieval for the small facts and rely on the model to infer them from the wording of the question
Use static retrieval for the small always-needed facts and dynamic retrieval for the large occasional history

stem: An assistant retrieves user memories dynamically through a lookup tool on Lakebase. Traces show that on questions about the user's earlier decisions, the agent answers directly without calling the tool, so personalization is missing. Which change addresses this with the least extra context?

choices.text: Make the tool description say what it returns and when to call it, or preload only the small always-needed fields statically
Replace the tool with a larger system prompt that repeats every memory category in full each turn
Remove the lookup tool and ask the model to recall earlier decisions from its general training knowledge
Preload all stored memories for the user into every prompt so that the tool is never needed at all

stem: A travel agent injects the 25 closest memories from its Lakebase-backed memory store into every request. As the store grew, answers got worse: asked to rebook a flight, the agent quoted a seat preference from a hotel stay two years ago and ignored the new date. The trace shows only 3 of the 25 injected memories relate to flights. Which diagnosis and fix fit best?

choices.text: Under-retrieval, because the agent ignored the new date, so raise the number of injected memories until the date appears again
A weak embedding model, so re-embed the whole memory store with a larger model and keep injecting all 25 closest memories
Over-retrieval that pollutes the window, so cap the injected memories and require a relevance score before a memory enters the prompt
Context clash, because the memories contradict each other, so delete the older memories and keep only the newest 25 entries

stem: A meal-planning agent recalls memories through a lookup that returns only items whose similarity score passes a very strict threshold. A user said in an earlier conversation, "I'm vegetarian," and the fact is in the memory store. In a new conversation the agent proposes a steak dinner. The trace shows the memory search span returned zero results for "what should I cook tonight". What is the failure and the best change?

choices.text: A pipeline delay, so schedule the memory pipeline to run more often and then re-run the same strict retrieval afterwards
Under-retrieval, so relax the threshold or query with the user's constraints, then confirm the memory returns
Memory poisoning, so rewrite the stored fact as an instruction in the system prompt and delete the entry from the memory store for good
Over-retrieval, so lower the number of results returned and keep the strict threshold so fewer memories are used

stem: An engineer compares two agent traces to tell over-retrieval from under-retrieval in a memory system. Which TWO observations point to over-retrieval? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The memory search returns one item, and the answer uses it correctly and cites the right detail
The memory search returns no items, and the agent asks the user for a preference already in the store
The answer lacks a fact that exists in the store but was missing from the list the memory search returned
The memory search returns twenty items, only two are used in the answer, and an unrelated item's detail appears in the response
The input tokens of each model call keep rising as the memory store grows, although the questions and the configured result count are unchanged in kind

stem: To stop context pollution, a team cuts memory retrieval from 10 results to 2. The evaluation dataset now shows fewer unrelated details in answers, but questions that need three separate stored facts (diet, budget, dates) lose accuracy. Which next step best balances both failures?

choices.text: Return to 10 results and accept the pollution, since recall failures are always more damaging than extra tokens
Keep 2 results and ask users to repeat the missing facts, since the store cannot support multi-fact questions
Set a relevance score gate with a moderate cap, then re-run the same evaluation to check both unrelated details and missing facts
Run the memory search a second time for every question and inject both result sets, doubling the retrieved text on each turn

stem: A wellness agent stores each past conversation transcript as one memory entry. For a question about the user's sleep goal, retrieval returns three entries that are about two thousand tokens each; the goal is a single sentence inside one of them. Most of the returned text is unrelated chat. Which change reduces over-retrieval without losing the goal?

choices.text: Distill conversations into short durable facts, one entry per goal, and retrieve those instead of whole transcripts
Make each stored entry larger so the goal and its surrounding conversation are always retrieved together as one block
Return a single transcript entry per question and hope the closest one contains the goal sentence
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore unrelated chat inside each retrieved memory entry

stem: A shopping agent's memory pipeline runs nightly. After months of use, one customer's memory store holds about forty near-identical entries such as "prefers aisle seats" and "likes aisle seat", and retrieval of the top five fills with these copies while the customer's allergy note ranks sixth and never reaches the prompt. Which change fits best?

choices.text: Have the memory pipeline consolidate duplicate facts into one durable entry each when it distills the sessions
Raise the retrieval count to fifty, so that the allergy note is always among the injected memories
Add a system prompt line telling the model that repeated preferences are not important to the customer
Delete the whole memory store each week and let the agent rebuild its preferences from new chats

stem: An engineer deletes an entire session store that belonged to a retired version of a support agent, to clean up. A product owner worries that every user's saved preferences will disappear and that the agent will start over with each person. What actually happens?

choices.text: Preferences stay but become read-only until a new session store with the same name is created
Preferences are lost, because memory is stored as a child object of the session store and is removed with it
Preferences stay, because deleting a session or a session store does not delete memory kept in a memory store
Preferences are lost, because the memory pipeline automatically rebuilds the memory store from sessions that no longer exist

stem: A shopping agent writes memories keyed by the current chat ID. A customer who set a size preference on Monday opens a new chat on Wednesday, and the agent shows no knowledge of it, although the memory entry exists. What configuration change fixes the recall?

choices.text: Make the embeddings more precise so Monday's chat ID is matched against Wednesday's chat ID
Retain each chat longer, so Wednesday's chat can load Monday's chat in full as its session state
Write the preference again at the start of each chat with a tool call, so every chat holds its own copy
Scope memories to the customer as the subject rather than to a chat, so any later conversation can recall them

stem: A team is starting a new agent that needs sessions and long-term memory on Databricks. Their wiki recommends the earlier managed agent memory store governed by Unity Catalog. Which choice matches current Databricks guidance for a new agent?

choices.text: Use the earlier managed memory store, because Unity Catalog governance makes it the recommended memory approach
Use Lakebase-backed agent sessions and agent memory, with a memory pipeline to distill sessions into memories
Build both on Delta files only, because Lakebase-backed stores cannot be used with other frameworks
Store memories as rows in the agent's own prompt template so that no store needs configuring

stem: A multi-tenant support agent keeps durable memories for thousands of customers in Databricks agent memory. Security requires that a customer's memories are only ever recalled for that customer and that only the right identities can touch the stores. Which TWO configuration practices satisfy this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Give all agents read access to every store so that a future agent can reuse any memory without a new grant
Merge the session store and the memory store into one store so that a single permission covers both
Put every customer's memories in one shared space and instruct the model in the prompt never to mention other customers
Grant access to the session and memory stores only to the identities that need them, using the store permission controls
Scope each memory to the customer as its subject and recall only that subject's memories when a request arrives

stem: In a support agent, a user writes "What did they decide about it?" after discussing a vendor contract earlier in the same conversation. The agent embeds the raw message, searches memory and receives unrelated items about other vendors. Where in the pipeline should the fix be applied?

choices.text: Resolve the intent first by using the session to turn "they" and "it" into a standalone query, then retrieve
Let the model read all returned items first and silently pick the right vendor from them
Increase the number of memories retrieved so that the right vendor decision is more likely to be among them
Fine-tune the embedding model on short messages that contain pronouns, such as "they" and "it"

stem: An engineer sketches four stages for an agent that answers from memory and tables. Which order puts intent resolution where the exam expects it?

choices.text: Receive message, retrieve with the raw text, inject the results, resolve intent from what was retrieved
Resolve intent from the retrieved items, receive the message, inject the results, retrieve with the raw text
Receive message with session state, resolve intent, retrieve with the resolved query, inject the results
Receive message, inject the entire memory store, retrieve what remains useful, resolve intent last

stem: An assistant is asked, "Show me the numbers for Apollo." The company has both a project and a customer called Apollo. Retrieval returns budget memos for the project and billing notes for the customer, and the answer blends them. The conversation gives no hint which is meant. What is the best fix in the pipeline?

choices.text: Add a metadata column labelled "apollo" to every document so that retrieval can match both meanings more exactly
Detect the ambiguity at the intent stage and ask a clarifying question or use session context before retrieving
Retrieve both sets, then add a system prompt line that tells the model to pick whichever Apollo seems more likely, and answer
Increase the result count so the answer can quote both Apollos and let the user sort out the mix

stem: A team adds an intent-resolution step to their memory agent. Which TWO benefits can they expect from resolving intent before retrieval? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The memory pipeline can store raw transcripts, since intent resolution cleans them at write time
Retrieval no longer needs evaluating, because a resolved query always returns exactly the right memories
The agent can route a request to the right source, such as a structured query for a stored field or semantic search for a vague recollection
The agent can answer without retrieving at all, because every question is understood well enough to guess
The retrieval query matches what the user means, so fewer irrelevant memories are pulled into the window

stem: A team adds a model call that rewrites every user message into a standalone query before memory retrieval. Latency rose noticeably. Their logs show that most messages are already self-contained, such as "What is my current plan tier?", while a minority use pronouns or name clashes. What is the best adjustment?

choices.text: Keep the model call but cache each rewrite for a year, so repeated messages never trigger a new call
Move the rewrite after retrieval so it can use the returned memories to decide what the user meant
Remove the resolution step entirely, since most messages do not need it and the few that do are acceptable losses
Run resolution only for ambiguous messages, such as unresolved references or several matches, and retrieve directly otherwise

stem: An agent connects to three MCP servers: a GitHub server, a Slack server and a custom server on Databricks Apps. Together they expose dozens of tools, and the trace shows every model call starting with all tool names, descriptions and parameter schemas, most of which are never used in a request. Which change applies progressive disclosure best?

choices.text: Remove two of the three servers from the agent for good and keep the one used most often
Show a short server catalog with each one's purpose, then load a server's tool schemas only when the agent picks it
Cut every tool description to one word so the same full list costs fewer tokens in each call
Move the full tool list into the system prompt so that the model provider can cache it across calls, keeping every tool

stem: A finance agent calls a generic SQL tool on a custom MCP server for "Which three regions had the highest gross margin last quarter?". The tool returns about four thousand transaction rows, which the model then sorts and totals itself, and the answer is sometimes wrong. What change cuts the tokens most while keeping the result reliable?

choices.text: Add a tool that aggregates and ranks in the warehouse and returns only the three regions with their margins
Compress the four thousand rows into a compact text table before they are returned, and let the model total it
Raise the tool's row limit so that the model always sees every transaction of the quarter
Ask the model in the system prompt to total each region carefully and double-check its sums

stem: An order-lookup tool on an MCP server returns a 60-field JSON record for each of up to 50 orders. The agent usually needs only the status of one order, but the trace shows the whole result sitting in the window for the rest of the conversation. How should the tool be redesigned to apply progressive disclosure to its output?

choices.text: Truncate the JSON after the first 2,000 characters so every result is the same length for every order
Increase the context window setting so that the large result fits and leaves more room for new messages
Ask the model in the prompt to ignore the unneeded fields once the result has been returned
Return a compact list of order IDs and statuses, plus a separate detail call for one chosen order

stem: A support agent is connected to a registered MCP server with 30 tools. The agent's callers can use only 18 of them under their Unity Catalog permissions. The trace shows the model choosing a tool it is not allowed to call, getting a permission error and retrying, and the 12 unusable definitions sit in every call. What is the best change?

choices.text: Grant every caller access to all 30 tools so that no tool call ever returns a permission error
Tell the agent in the prompt which 12 tools are unavailable and to skip them each time it plans
Restrict the tools exposed to this agent to the 18 its callers may use, so the other 12 are never loaded
Add a retry loop that moves on to the next tool whenever a call comes back with a permission error

stem: After switching to a tool catalog, an agent that answers customer chats loads tool schemas only on demand. Latency increased, because the same five tools, such as order lookup and refund, are used in almost every chat and each now needs an extra step to load. Which design keeps most of the savings?

choices.text: Keep the five common tools fully loaded and put the rarely used ones behind the catalog
Disclose every tool progressively, as designed, and accept the added round trip for all of them
Load every tool schema up front again, because latency matters more than context cost
Add more tools to the catalog so the agent can find a shortcut for common requests

stem: An agent has two MCP tools. `find_customer` is described as "Looks up customer information." `get_account` is described as "Retrieves account information for a customer." The agent calls them almost at random for questions such as "What is the billing address for Dana Lee?" Which change fixes the confusion?

choices.text: Add the same example call to the system prompt for both tools so the model sees how each is called
Rewrite each description to state what it returns, its key input and when to use it instead of the other tool
Rename the two tools `tool_a` and `tool_b` so the names cannot suggest anything misleading
Append all synonyms of "customer" and "account" to both descriptions so every question matches strongly

stem: A billing agent has four MCP tools. `get_invoice`: "Returns billing documents for a customer, including invoices and credit notes." `list_payments`: "Returns payment transactions for a customer, including refunds." `get_billing_history`: "Returns billing documents and payments for a customer." `get_shipment_status`: "Returns the current delivery status of a shipment." The agent often picks the wrong tool for billing questions. Where is the overlap?

choices.text: `get_invoice` and `get_shipment_status` overlap, because both return documents and statuses about a customer's orders
`list_payments` and `get_shipment_status` overlap, because both return a status-like result
There is no overlap, because every tool has a different name and returns a different noun
`get_billing_history` overlaps `get_invoice` and `list_payments`, because it describes the union of their outputs

stem: Two tools from different MCP servers are called `search_docs` ("Finds relevant documents") and `search_wiki` ("Finds relevant articles"). The agent uses them interchangeably, sometimes missing the right answer. Which TWO edits remove the overlap? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Add the sentence "Use whichever seems best" to both descriptions so that the model decides for itself
Describe both tools with the same longer text so they are equally likely to be chosen for every question
State the source and content type of each, such as policy PDFs in a volume versus engineering wiki pages
Rename them `search1` and `search2` so that the names carry no meaning that could bias the choice
Add an explicit boundary to each, such as "For team how-to pages use `search_wiki` instead"

stem: An agent is connected to GitHub and Slack MCP servers. Each exposes a tool called `search` described as "Searches for items matching a query." The agent sometimes searches Slack when the user asks about code. Which fix addresses the overlap?

choices.text: Add a rule to the system prompt that says the agent must always try Slack search before GitHub search
Make names and descriptions say which system and item types each searches, such as issues versus messages
Add a retry loop so a wrong search is repeated against the other server until some results come back
Remove one server from the agent and add the missing search by hand later

stem: An agent has `get_customer(id STRING)` and `get_account(id STRING)`. Both parameter descriptions read "The id." The tool descriptions differ, yet traces show the agent passing account numbers to `get_customer` and customer IDs to `get_account`. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Describe each parameter's meaning and format, such as customer ID `C-` plus digits and account `ACC-` plus digits
Keep more example tool calls in the history so the model can copy earlier correct calls
Add a validation step in the system prompt that asks the model to double-check every id it fills in before each call
Merge both tools into `get_record(id STRING)` and let the backend guess which kind of id it received

stem: An analytics agent can reach 60 registered tools. Its traces show that every model call starts with the full name, description and parameter schema of all 60 tools, and most of the attention budget is gone before the user's question is read. The team adopts progressive disclosure for tools. What does the context window hold at the first stage, before the agent has picked a tool?

choices.text: Only the user's question, with no tool information at all, so the agent must guess a tool name and wait for an error to learn its parameters
The full schemas of the ten most frequently used tools, with the remaining fifty tools hidden until the agent asks for them by exact name
The full schema of every tool, compressed by removing parameter descriptions so that all 60 tools still fit in a smaller footprint
A compact index of tool names with one-line descriptions, while the full parameter schema of a tool is added only after the agent selects it

stem: A support agent connects to several tool servers. To apply progressive disclosure, an engineer must add something to the agent so that it can move from the light tool index to the full definition of one tool. Which design supplies that step?

choices.text: Add a lookup step the agent calls with a tool name to receive that tool's full schema
Remove tools from the index after their first use so the model sees each definition only once
Rewrite the system prompt to list all tool schemas in a collapsible section the model is told to ignore until needed
Increase the index descriptions to hold every parameter name and type so the agent never needs a second step

stem: A team reviews how an agent's window should look under progressive disclosure for tools. Which TWO statements describe the intended behavior? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Disclosure is complete after the first stage, because a name and a one-line description are enough to fill every argument
The tool index is regenerated by the model from memory at the start of each turn, so no tool list is stored anywhere
Before a tool is chosen, the window carries only a short entry per tool, and the full schema of a tool appears only after it is selected
Every tool's full schema stays loaded for the whole session so that the agent can switch tools without any extra step
The number of tool tokens in the window grows with the tools the agent actually uses, not with the number of tools that exist

stem: An agent uses a tool index plus a schema lookup tool. Traces show that it picks the right tool from the index, then calls it at once with guessed argument names and gets validation errors, while the lookup tool is almost never called. The index lines and the lookup tool both work correctly. What change fixes this with the least added context?

choices.text: Put every tool's full parameter schema back into the index lines so that no second step is needed to find the argument names
State the protocol in the system prompt: pick from the index, call the lookup for that tool's schema, and only then call the tool
Retry each failed call automatically up to five times so that the agent finds the right argument names through trial and error
Add three worked example calls for every tool to the system prompt so that the agent can copy the argument names from them

stem: A catalog has 60 tools. A full schema costs about 500 tokens and an index line about 20 tokens. A typical request needs 3 tools, and the agent uses a lookup call for each. Which estimate of the tool tokens per model call is right once the 3 schemas are loaded, and what is the main cost of staging?

choices.text: About 1,200 tokens, because only the index counts once the schemas are loaded on demand, and there are no extra round trips
About 15,000 tokens, because staging halves the cost of a tool dump whatever the size of the catalog and the request
About 31,200 tokens, because the index is added on top of the full schemas, so staging raises the cost per call for large catalogs
About 2,700 tokens, roughly 90% below the 30,000-token full dump, paid for with one lookup round trip per tool the agent uses

stem: A research agent is close to its context limit. The history holds a 30,000-character JSON result from `get_orders`, returned 25 turns ago. Since then, the agent has written the three order ids and totals it needed into its running plan, and it will not use the raw JSON again. Which action frees space without hurting the task?

choices.text: Clear the raw `get_orders` result, keep the plan entries and leave a short note of the call
Truncate the JSON to its first 2,000 characters so that part of every old result remains available to the model
Clear the assistant's reasoning messages from the last ten turns, since reasoning is less important than tool data
Delete the plan entries along with the JSON, because the plan also repeats information that the JSON already contained

stem: An analyst agent nears its window limit. Which TWO tool results are the best candidates for clearing? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A 200-token result holding the refund confirmation number that the final answer must report and that no note records
A 14,000-token result of a broad query that the agent later replaced with a narrower query whose result is also in the history
A 5,000-token result returned by the call the agent made one step ago and has not yet analyzed
A 300-token result giving the user's region, which each of the remaining steps uses as a filter
A 9,000-token column listing for 40 tables, after the agent chose two tables and wrote their column names into its notes

stem: An inventory agent calls `get_stock` at each step and must diff the newest result against the previous two. After 40 steps the history is near its limit, mostly from 40 results of about 3,000 tokens each. Results older than the previous two are never compared again. Which clearing policy fits?

choices.text: Clear the three newest results and keep the oldest 37, because older results were checked by more steps
Keep every result for the whole task, because any old snapshot might be needed for some later diff
Keep the three newest results in full and replace older ones with placeholders naming the call and key figures
Clear all 40 results right after each is read, so that every diff has to be rebuilt from a stored summary

stem: After a team enabled clearing of old tool outputs, an agent started to call `get_inventory` again and again on long tasks, even though the result had already been seen and used. The traces show that the cleared results vanish completely from the history. What change fixes the repeated calls?

choices.text: Instruct the agent in the prompt to avoid calling any tool more than once per conversation
Clear results more often so that the model never has time to notice which calls were made
Disable clearing completely, because removing old outputs from the history always causes an agent to repeat its tool calls
Leave a placeholder for each cleared result naming the tool, arguments and key facts

stem: A data-analysis agent runs queries whose raw results are written by the tool to a Delta table and also returned to the agent as long result sets. The history is near its limit. The analyst may later need to re-examine the rows. How should the agent clear the old results?

choices.text: Keep the newest result sets in full and delete older ones, leaving no record of where they were stored
Replace each large result with a placeholder holding the table name, row count and key findings
Summarize the full history into prose and discard the table, so that the rows are only recoverable from the summary
Move the raw rows from the Delta table into the system prompt, where they will never be cleared by the framework

stem: An agent finishes an order check and must compute a discount. It has already extracted `order_total` (a decimal number) and `tier` (a string such as "gold") from earlier steps. Two Unity Catalog functions are registered as tools: `get_order(order_id STRING)` returns the full order row, and `calc_discount(order_total DOUBLE, tier STRING)` returns the discount as a DOUBLE. Which tool fits the step?

choices.text: `calc_discount`, because its inputs are values the agent already holds and its output is the number the step needs
`get_order`, because retrieving the whole order row gives the agent every value it might need for the discount
`get_order`, called twice so that the second result can confirm the discount stored on the first row
Neither, because a discount is arithmetic and a registered function should never be used for arithmetic

stem: A scheduling agent needs a start time for `book_meeting`, which accepts `start_time STRING` in ISO 8601 form such as "2026-11-09T14:00:00Z". Three registered functions could supply a time. Which design is compatible with it?

choices.text: `next_free_slot_epoch()`, which returns an integer count of seconds since 1970, because integers are never ambiguous or locale dependent
`next_free_slot_epoch()`, with the model asked to convert the integer into the ISO string before booking
`next_free_slot_iso()`, which returns a STRING in ISO 8601 UTC format, so the value can be passed to `book_meeting` unchanged
`next_free_slot_local()`, which returns a free-text string like "Tuesday afternoon" that people find easy to read

stem: Every Monday an agent must report revenue for one region and one quarter, always using the finance team's approved calculation. Only the region and the quarter change between requests. Which registered tool design best fits?

choices.text: A web search tool, so the agent can find a published revenue formula to use each time
A Unity Catalog SQL function with `region` and `quarter` parameters wrapping the approved query, registered as the agent's tool
A tool that accepts any SQL text, so the agent can write the revenue query itself each Monday
A tool that returns the whole revenue table for all regions and quarters, with the agent filtering the rows for the requested region itself

stem: An agent must look up a customer's open tickets by status. Two registered functions both return tickets. `tickets_by_filter(filter STRING)` expects a free-text expression such as "status = 'open' AND ..." typed by the caller. `tickets_by_status(customer_id STRING, status STRING)` takes the customer id and one status value, documented as one of 'open', 'pending' or 'closed'. Which is the better choice for the agent and why?

choices.text: `tickets_by_status`, because the typed inputs and the allowed values reduce malformed calls and keep arguments small
`tickets_by_filter`, because a free-text expression can express any condition the user may think of
Both are equally suitable, because the model will generate correct arguments for either function
`tickets_by_filter`, because a single string parameter is easier for the model to fill than two named parameters with allowed values

stem: An agent must tell a user whether a single shipment has been delivered. Three registered functions could be used. `shipments_all()` returns every shipment record. `shipment_detail(id)` returns a 60-field record with full event history. `shipment_status(id)` returns one STRING such as "DELIVERED". Which is the best match for the task?

choices.text: `shipment_detail(id)`, called once at the beginning of each conversation and kept in the window for later turns
`shipment_detail(id)`, because the full event history lets the agent reason about the delivery on its own
`shipment_status(id)`, because it returns exactly the value needed and avoids filling the window with unneeded fields
`shipments_all()`, because with every record in the window the agent can answer any follow-up question

stem: A team keeps a 1,500-word "PII handling" procedure in its agent's system prompt: steps for masking columns, a naming convention for masked views and a reusable script. Only about one request in ten involves PII, but every request pays for the text. What should the team do?

choices.text: Split the procedure into ten parts and place one part in the prompt of each of ten requests
Move the procedure into a tool description, so that it is part of the tool list on every call
Shorten the procedure to a single sentence in the system prompt and drop the script, because long procedures confuse models
Package the procedure, its examples and its script as an Agent Skill so that it is loaded only for requests where it is relevant

stem: An engineer is building a custom Agent Skill for a Databricks coding agent. Which TWO statements describe how a skill is built? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The skill is a single text field pasted into the system prompt, with no file structure and no description
Every skill's full instructions are loaded into each conversation, whether or not the request relates to them
Longer reference material and scripts can sit in extra files in the skill folder and be referenced with relative paths
The skill must contain only prose, since scripts and extra files cannot be added to a skill

stem: A platform team decides what goes into the agent's always-on system prompt and what becomes an Agent Skill. Which requirement belongs in the system prompt rather than in a skill?

choices.text: A set of Delta pipeline templates that only the data engineering team needs for new pipelines
A multi-step workflow for tuning a model's training run, with scripts and example outputs
A weekly procedure for building a release-notes document from a standard template, used by two engineers on the platform team
The rule that every answer must follow the company's tone and must never reveal internal project code names

stem: A team packaged its data-quality workflow as a skill whose description reads "Helpful workflow stuff." Users report that the agent either ignores the skill for data-quality requests or sometimes applies it to unrelated tasks. The `SKILL.md` instructions themselves are correct. What fixes the loading behavior?

choices.text: Move every referenced script into `SKILL.md` so that the skill loads as a single file
Rewrite the name and description so that they state what the skill does and when it should be used, keeping the skill focused on one workflow
Copy the instructions into the system prompt as well, so that the agent has them whatever the description says
Merge this skill with the team's other skills into one large skill so that the agent has a single description to match

stem: A debugging agent's history is compacted by a summarization prompt. After compaction the agent repeatedly asks the user for the exact stack trace and the file path it had already seen. The summaries read well but contain phrases like "an error occurred in the loader". Which change to the compaction prompt best addresses the problem?

choices.text: Instruct the summarizer to keep error messages, stack traces, file paths and identifiers verbatim and compress only the narrative
Tell the summarizer to keep a friendly narrative tone so that the agent can follow the story of the session
Move compaction earlier so that it runs when the history is much shorter and has fewer details to lose
Ask the summarizer to produce a shorter summary so that the compacted history leaves more room for new turns

stem: A migration agent was told in turn 3: "Do not touch the `orders_prod` table; work only in `orders_dev`." After the history was compacted, the agent ran a write against `orders_prod`. The summary only said "the user asked for a migration of the orders tables." What should the team change in the compaction step?

choices.text: Increase the model's sampling temperature so the agent tries different actions after compaction
Delete every user message from the summary input, since the user's messages are the source of conflicting instructions
Add the sentence "be careful with production tables" to the system prompt and leave the compaction prompt as it is
Add a rule that compaction must keep the user's current goal, constraints and prohibitions, stated explicitly in the summary

stem: A research agent keeps repeating an approach that already failed, and re-asks the user for a customer id given earlier, after each compaction. A review of the summaries shows they keep conclusions but drop two kinds of information. Which TWO additions to the compaction prompt target these losses? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Require a short list of approaches already tried and why each failed, so the agent does not retry them
Require the summary to be written in the third person, with no names or numbers, to protect privacy
Ask the summarizer to sort the summary by timestamp and to list every single message it replaces
Ask the summarizer to remove any mention of failed attempts, so the agent does not dwell on mistakes
Require identifiers and values supplied by the user or tools, such as the customer id, to be kept exactly as given

stem: A long-running agent's compacted summaries are accurate but, after each compaction, the agent stops and asks "what should I do next?" even though a multi-step plan was in progress. Comparing the raw history with the summary shows that the plan's remaining steps were dropped. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Add a second summarization pass that shortens the first summary further, so only the outcome remains
Add to the compaction prompt a required section for current state and remaining steps, in the order the agent planned to do them
Ask the summarizer to describe the history in more detail by quoting each tool result in full
Disable compaction and let the history grow until the model's window overflows, then restart the task from the beginning

stem: A finance agent compacts its history. After compaction, it reports "revenue improved strongly in the second quarter" but the user's later question about the exact growth rate cannot be answered, because the agent only has that sentence. The raw history had the figures from the query results. What should the team do first?

choices.text: Replace compaction with deleting the oldest half of the history, since deleted turns can never be summarized wrongly or distort any numbers
Add a rule to the system prompt that the agent must not answer any question about growth rates
Confirm from the raw history that figures were dropped, then make the compaction prompt keep exact figures with units and labels
Ask the summarizer to round all numbers to the nearest integer to make the summary easier to read
